chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from al-Barqi from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira from Amr ibn Thabit from Abdullah ibn Aqil ibn Abi Talib said:

Two men differed regarding the case of Ali and Umar concerning a woman whom her husband had divorced with one or two divorces, then another man married her, and he either divorced her or died, so when her waiting period ended, the first husband married her. Umar said: 'She is upon what remains of the divorce.' Ali (peace be upon him) said: 'Glory be to Allah, does three [divorces] not annul [the bond], and one [divorce] not annul [it]?' (Implying that if three divorces are required to make her fully permissible again, one should suffice to return her to the first husband without a new marriage contract, or conversely, that the logic of 'annulment' applies equally).
ai.seo_question: What is the difference between Umar and Ali's rulings on a woman divorced once or twice who marries another man and then returns to the first husband?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Istibsar* highlights the jurisprudential divergence between Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ali ibn Abi Talib regarding the status of a woman in *Tanzil al-Katimah* (divorced three times, then married and divorced/died by a second husband) when the first husband seeks to remarry her. While Umar maintained that the initial three divorces remained binding (preventing immediate remarriage without a new contract), Ali argued for the nullification of the previous count, asserting that the intervening marriage severed the legal tie, thus allowing the first husband to remarry her as if no prior divorce had occurred. This narration is central to the Shia debate on whether the 'three divorces' rule is a permanent barrier or a conditional one dependent on the consummation of the intervening marriage.
